item.title: Nijo Castle Guide: The Shogun's Palace & Nightingale Floors
item.description: Nijo Castle is where the power of the shogun was put on display — and, three centuries later, where it was formally surrendered. Built by the Tokugawa shoguns as their Kyoto residence, it is not a fortress of soaring keeps but a sprawling palace of tatami halls, gold-leaf screens, ornate carved transoms, and gardens, surrounded by moats and stone walls. Walking its Ninomaru Palace — across floors deliberately engineered to “sing” like nightingales to warn of intruders — is one of the most evocative historical experiences in Kyoto, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

item.title: Ryukyu Gusuku Guide: Zakimi Castle & UNESCO Ruins
item.description: Long before Shuri unified the islands, Okinawa was dotted with gusuku — the fortified castles of rival Ryukyu lords. Several of their dramatic ruins, prized for their flowing, beautifully engineered curved limestone walls, are inscribed together as UNESCO World Heritage (“Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu”). Zakimi Castle in Yomitan is among the most accessible and best preserved, its ramparts open to walk and offering views to the sea.

item.title: Shiretoko Peninsula Guide: UNESCO Nature, Cruises & Bears
item.description: Jutting into the Sea of Okhotsk at Hokkaido’s far northeast, the Shiretoko Peninsula is one of Japan’s last great wildernesses — a UNESCO World Heritage site where primeval forest, volcanic peaks and a wild coast of cliffs and waterfalls shelter an extraordinary density of wildlife. This is brown bear country, home also to deer, foxes, eagles and, offshore, whales and seals. Explore the Shiretoko Five Lakes, take a nature cruise beneath sea cliffs, and in late winter watch drift ice pack the shore.

item.title: Shuri Castle Guide: Tickets, Reconstruction & Access (Naha)
item.description: Shuri Castle (Shurijō) was the political and ceremonial heart of the Ryukyu Kingdom for some 450 years, and remains Okinawa’s most important historic site. With its distinctive vermilion halls, Chinese- and Japanese-influenced architecture, and hilltop views over Naha, it is a UNESCO World Heritage component (“Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu”). A devastating fire in October 2019 destroyed the main hall (Seiden) and several structures; the castle is now in the midst of a multi-year reconstruction, which has itself become a fascinating thing to witness.

item.title: Yanbaru Guide: UNESCO Forest, Wildlife & Access
item.description: The lush, mountainous north of Okinawa Island is Yanbaru — a subtropical forest so biodiverse it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage natural site in 2021. Home to rare endemic creatures found nowhere else on Earth, like the flightless Okinawa rail (Yanbaru kuina) and the Okinawa woodpecker, it offers a completely different Okinawa from the beaches: dense green ridges, waterfalls, mangroves and the dramatic karst formations of Daisekirinzan. It’s the island’s premier destination for nature lovers.

item.title: Gifu Top Sightseeing: Shirakawa-go, Takayama & Cormorant Fishing
item.description: Gifu Prefecture occupies the mountainous heart of Honshu, a landlocked expanse of deep valleys, ancient cedar forests, and river gorges that stretches from the Northern Alps down to the Nobi Plain. It is a prefecture of genuine superlatives: one of Japan’s three great onsen towns, a UNESCO World Heritage village that looks unchanged from the eighteenth century, a mountain town preserved so completely that it earned the name Little Kyoto of the Alps, and a cormorant fishing tradition that has continued unbroken for thirteen hundred years.

item.title: Shirakawa-go Complete Guide: UNESCO Thatched Villages in the Mountains
item.description: In the mountains of northern Gifu, where the Japan Alps trap winter snowfall in depths that would overwhelm an ordinary building, a style of farmhouse evolved over centuries that turns the problem into architecture. The gassho-zukuri farmhouses of Shirakawa-go — their steeply pitched thatched roofs rising three to five storeys, angled like hands pressed together in prayer — are among the most recognisable structures in Japan, and among the few historic building traditions still inhabited and maintained by the communities that created them.

item.title: Noto Peninsula Road Trip Guide: Senmaida, Wajima & the Sea of Japan Coast
item.description: The Noto Peninsula extends northward from Kanazawa into the Sea of Japan like a finger pointing toward the Korean coast — a narrow strip of land, roughly 60 kilometres from base to tip, whose distance from any large city has preserved a way of life that has disappeared from most of rural Japan. Here, fishing communities still operate according to seasonal rhythms set centuries ago. Traditional farm families maintain the terraced rice paddies that cascade down hillsides to the sea.
